title: Exactness on each graded piece of the symmetric algebra of a quotient
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, and for an $R$-module $N$ let $\operatorname{Sym}_R(N)=\mathrm T_R(N)/(x\otimes y-y\otimes x)$ be its symmetric algebra, the quotient of the tensor algebra $\mathrm T_R(N)=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}N^{\otimes_R k}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the elements $x\otimes y-y\otimes x$ ($x,y\in N$), with canonical $R$-linear map $\iota_N:N\to\operatorname{Sym}_R(N)$ [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property], and for $k\ge0$ let $\operatorname{Sym}^k_R(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}_R(N)$ be its degree-$k$ part, the image of $N^{\otimes_R k}$, i.e. the $R$-submodule spanned by the products $\iota_N(x_1)\cdots\iota_N(x_k)$ ($\operatorname{Sym}^0_R(N)=R\cdot1$) [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-graded]. Let $M_2\xrightarrow{\;a\;}M_1\xrightarrow{\;p\;}M\to0$ be an exact sequence of $R$-modules (so $p$ is surjective and $\ker p=\operatorname{im}a$), and let $\operatorname{Sym}(p):\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)\to\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$ be the $R$-algebra homomorphism with $\operatorname{Sym}(p)(\iota_{M_1}(x))=\iota_M(p(x))$ for $x\in M_1$. Let $n\ge1$. Then $\operatorname{Sym}(p)$ maps $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ into $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$; let $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p):\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)\to\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$ be its restriction. There is a unique $R$-linear map $\varphi_n:M_2\otimes_R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}_R(M_1)\to\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ with $\varphi_n(y\otimes s)=\iota_{M_1}(a(y))\cdot s$, and the sequence $$M_2\otimes_R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}_R(M_1)\xrightarrow{\;\varphi_n\;}\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)\xrightarrow{\;\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)\;}\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)\to0$$ is exact: $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$ is surjective and $\ker\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)=\operatorname{im}\varphi_n$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DO (lemma-presentation-sym-exterior, line 2241), the degree-n exact sequence for an exact sequence M_2 -> M_1 -> M -> 0

proof.text: (The maps.) By the universal property [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property] applied to the $R$-linear map $\iota_M\circ p:M_1\to\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$ there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism $\operatorname{Sym}(p)$ with $\operatorname{Sym}(p)\circ\iota_{M_1}=\iota_M\circ p$. Being multiplicative, it sends a product $\iota_{M_1}(x_1)\cdots\iota_{M_1}(x_n)$ to $\iota_M(p(x_1))\cdots\iota_M(p(x_n))\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$; since these products span $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-graded], $\operatorname{Sym}(p)(\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1))\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$, and $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$ is defined. The map $M_2\times\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}_R(M_1)\to\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)$, $(y,s)\mapsto\iota_{M_1}(a(y))\,s$, is $R$-bilinear (as $\iota_{M_1}$, $a$ are $R$-linear and $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)$ is an $R$-algebra) and takes values in $\operatorname{Sym}^1_R(M_1)\cdot\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}_R(M_1)\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-graded]; by the universal property of the tensor product it induces the unique $R$-linear $\varphi_n$ with $\varphi_n(y\otimes s)=\iota_{M_1}(a(y))s$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DO (lemma-presentation-sym-exterior, line 2241; proof omitted in the source); maps as in the statement there

proof.text: (Surjectivity of $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$.) $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$ is spanned by the products $\iota_M(m_1)\cdots\iota_M(m_n)$ with $m_i\in M$ [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-graded]. As $p$ is surjective choose $x_i\in M_1$ with $p(x_i)=m_i$; then $\iota_{M_1}(x_1)\cdots\iota_{M_1}(x_n)\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ and by Step 1 its image under $\operatorname{Sym}(p)$ is $\iota_M(m_1)\cdots\iota_M(m_n)$. So the image of the $R$-linear map $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$ contains a spanning set, and $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$ is surjective.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DO (lemma-presentation-sym-exterior, line 2241; proof omitted in the source); right exactness at Sym^n(M)

proof.text: (The composite is zero.) Let $I\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)$ be the ideal generated by $\iota_{M_1}(a(M_2))$. For $y\in M_2$, $\operatorname{Sym}(p)(\iota_{M_1}(a(y)))=\iota_M(p(a(y)))=\iota_M(0)=0$ because $p\circ a=0$ (exactness at $M_1$, $\operatorname{im}a\subseteq\ker p$). Hence $\operatorname{Sym}(p)$, a ring homomorphism, vanishes on the ideal $I$; in particular $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)(\varphi_n(y\otimes s))=\operatorname{Sym}(p)(\iota_{M_1}(a(y)))\operatorname{Sym}(p)(s)=0$, so $\operatorname{im}\varphi_n\subseteq\ker\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DO (lemma-presentation-sym-exterior, line 2241; proof omitted in the source)

proof.text: (The kernel of $\operatorname{Sym}(p)$ is $I$.) Let $Q=\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)/I$, a commutative $R$-algebra, with quotient map $q$. By Step 3, $\operatorname{Sym}(p)$ factors as $\bar\sigma\circ q$ for an $R$-algebra homomorphism $\bar\sigma:Q\to\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$. Define $g:M\to Q$ by $g(p(x))=q(\iota_{M_1}(x))$: this is well defined since $p$ is surjective and, if $p(x)=p(x')$, then $x-x'\in\ker p=\operatorname{im}a$ (exactness at $M_1$), say $x-x'=a(y)$, so $q(\iota_{M_1}(x))-q(\iota_{M_1}(x'))=q(\iota_{M_1}(a(y)))=0$; it is $R$-linear because $p$, $\iota_{M_1}$, $q$ are. The universal property [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property] gives an $R$-algebra homomorphism $\psi:\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)\to Q$ with $\psi\circ\iota_M=g$. Then (i) $\bar\sigma\circ\psi$ is an $R$-algebra endomorphism of $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M)$ with $\bar\sigma(\psi(\iota_M(p(x))))=\bar\sigma(q(\iota_{M_1}(x)))=\operatorname{Sym}(p)(\iota_{M_1}(x))=\iota_M(p(x))$, so it agrees with the identity on $\iota_M(M)$ ($p$ surjective) and equals the identity by the uniqueness clause of [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property]. (ii) $\psi\circ\bar\sigma\circ q$ and $q$ are $R$-algebra homomorphisms $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)\to Q$ into the commutative $R$-algebra $Q$ with $\psi(\bar\sigma(q(\iota_{M_1}(x))))=\psi(\iota_M(p(x)))=g(p(x))=q(\iota_{M_1}(x))$, so they agree on $\iota_{M_1}(M_1)$ and are equal by the same uniqueness; as $q$ is surjective, $\psi\circ\bar\sigma=\mathrm{id}_Q$. Thus $\bar\sigma$ is bijective, and $\ker\operatorname{Sym}(p)=\ker(\bar\sigma\circ q)=\ker q=I$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DO (lemma-presentation-sym-exterior, line 2241; proof omitted in the source); the source gives no proof, the argument identifies Sym(M) with Sym(M_1)/(image of M_2) through the universal property of Section 00DM (section-tensor-algebra, line 2165)

proof.text: (The degree-$n$ part of $I$.) Claim: $I\cap\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)=\operatorname{im}\varphi_n$. The inclusion $\supseteq$: $\varphi_n(y\otimes s)=\iota_{M_1}(a(y))s$ lies in $I$ and in $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ (Step 1). For $\subseteq$: since $\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)$ is commutative, every $z\in I$ is a finite sum $z=\sum_{i=1}^r\iota_{M_1}(a(y_i))\,t_i$ with $y_i\in M_2$, $t_i\in\operatorname{Sym}_R(M_1)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-graded] write $t_i=\sum_{k\ge0}t_{i,k}$ with $t_{i,k}\in\operatorname{Sym}^k_R(M_1)$ (finitely many nonzero). Then $z=\sum_{k\ge0}z_{k+1}$ with $z_{k+1}=\sum_i\iota_{M_1}(a(y_i))\,t_{i,k}\in\operatorname{Sym}^{k+1}_R(M_1)$ (as $\iota_{M_1}(a(y_i))\in\operatorname{Sym}^1_R(M_1)$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^1\cdot\operatorname{Sym}^k\subseteq\operatorname{Sym}^{k+1}$), and the degree-$0$ component of $z$ is $0$. If moreover $z\in\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$, uniqueness of the decomposition into homogeneous components [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-graded] gives $z=z_n=\sum_i\iota_{M_1}(a(y_i))\,t_{i,n-1}=\varphi_n\bigl(\sum_i y_i\otimes t_{i,n-1}\bigr)\in\operatorname{im}\varphi_n$ (here $n\ge1$ is used).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DO (lemma-presentation-sym-exterior, line 2241; proof omitted in the source); the ideal generated by degree-1 elements meets degree n in their products with degree n-1, by the grading of Section 00DM (line 2165)

proof.text: (Conclusion.) $\ker\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)=\ker\operatorname{Sym}(p)\cap\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)=I\cap\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)=\operatorname{im}\varphi_n$ by Steps 4 and 5, and $\operatorname{Sym}^n(p)$ is surjective by Step 2. So the sequence is exact at $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M_1)$ and at $\operatorname{Sym}^n_R(M)$.
